 Thrust Into NBA Whirlwind, Game Is Quickly Slowing Down For Christian Anderson Jr.
 Sam Perley November 17, 2026 1:34 PM EST The transition from college to the NBA is different for every incoming rookie player. For first-year point guard Christian Anderson Jr, he’s experienced his fair share of normal growing pains since getting tossed into the Charlotte Hornets’ rotation in the season opener back on Oct. 21. Yet less than three weeks later, it’s hard to argue how much more comfortable Anderson looks compared to his first handful of games in the league.
 Due to injuries to veterans Coby White and then Dennis Schröder, Anderson has played in all but one of the Hornets’ opening 13 games of the season. While the offensive efficiency wasn’t necessarily pretty over his first nine outings – 2.8 points on 28% shooting and 9% from 3-point range (2-of-22) – Anderson was getting quality looks, while finding other ways to contribute, particularly on the defensive end. Since this stretch though, the 20-year-old has posted a new career high for points in three consecutive games, resulting in averages of 12.7 points on 50% shooting, 3.3 3-pointers on 56% shooting and 1.7 assists across 17.3 reserve minutes.
 “For a young player to come in and have a lot thrown at you in terms of the NBA lifestyle [being] different, practices, role, terminology, all that stuff is very new to [Christian],” said Hornets Head Coach Charles Lee prior to Anderson’s career-high 16-point performance against the LA Clippers on Sunday afternoon. “I think he’s done a phenomenal job picking things up. I credit him and I credit his teammates. I see a ton of guys wanting to take the time to have individual one-on-one conversations with him, either during timeouts or during the game. Our coaching staff has been really active in trying to watch film and get him up to speed as best as possible.”
 “I think just being able to know what we want to run, being able to think the game a lot faster and not be sped up,” said Anderson, when asked about his most significant areas of growth. “Just like offensively, defensively, being able to dictate where people want to go and playing to the coverage and all that stuff. I think that’s the main thing about how you can really make the game a lot slower. [The vets are] helping me with what I need to know on the court. They’ve been super helpful just giving me insight and a lot of knowledge. They’ve been really helpful off the court, too with their leadership and leading by example.”
 This season, Anderson and Oklahoma City’s Bennett Stirtz are the only two rookies to make three-or-more 3-pointers on at least 50% shooting in three consecutive games, a feat accomplished by just two other players in Hornets’ franchise history (Kon Knueppel, Adam Morrison). Defensively, Anderson has registered a team-high 15 deflections over his past four games, bringing his seasonal total to 22 and moving him to eighth on the rookie leaderboard. 
 During his two collegiate seasons at Texas Tech, the 6-foot-1, 180-pound Anderson used his speed, agility and quickness to create open shots for himself and his teammates. Of course, the NBA is a whole different animal – the players are bigger, faster and stronger. Not to mention, Anderson is also now serving in a reserve role after starting all 33 games last season and is averaging less than half (5.3) of the nightly shot attempts (13.1) he put up with the Red Raiders. The decreased usage and minutes are a challenging adjustment for young players, but Anderson and his smooth shooting stroke have found a steady rhythm over his past few appearances.
 “Obviously, the [NBA] bodies are a lot more physical and it's a lot faster game,” said Anderson following Sunday’s outing. “I’ve just got to get used to being ready right away. When your name is called, you can't feel it out, like how you can in college a little bit. So, I think my biggest thing is just being ready when my name's called and getting used to the pressure and physicality.”
 Added Lee, “Defensively, even though [Christian] lacks size sometimes on the court, there’s a scrappiness to him, there’s a fight to him, there’s a competitive spirit where you’re watching him guard guys in the post… It’s because of some of the shift activity, but it’s also because Christian is scrappy… We just need more of that.”
 One key development for Anderson has been learning how to play aggressive when he’s off the ball or on defense without it being a detriment to himself or the team.
 “When he is at his best, [Christian’s] a very smart basketball player, but sometimes that can be a gift and a curse where you overthink things,” explained Lee. “Ultimately, we want him to go out there and be very aggressive. When you tell a young player that, it’s also good to tell him what aggressive means. That doesn’t always mean shooting – it could be physicality defensively or being aggressive at the point of attack. Then, offensively, if we play pick-and-roll, it’s making sure that the defense is having to guard you, commit to you, shift and then you’re making your passes – not just coming off early in the clock if you’re being pressured.”
 The Hornets have probably counted on Christian Anderson Jr. a bit more at this stage of the season than they expected heading into the campaign. And yet, despite the unexpected change of plans, things are beginning to click for the promising rookie as he stacks up reps and gains more exposure.
